name: Beta-alanine

lead: Beta-alanine is a non-proteinogenic amino acid and the rate-limiting building block of carnosine, a dipeptide stored in skeletal muscle. It is sold as a powder or capsule, often in pre-workout blends.

Athletes use it to improve performance in efforts lasting roughly one to four minutes and to get more work done in high-repetition sets. Studies report a modest effect that does not directly add muscle; the evidence base supports it as an ergogenic aid, and the wiki's rating is strong.

paras: Taking beta-alanine for several weeks raises muscle carnosine content. Carnosine helps buffer hydrogen ions that accumulate during intense exercise, which is proposed to delay fatigue. The familiar tingling (paraesthesia) comes from activation of sensory nerve receptors and is not considered an indicator of effect.

Paraesthesia is the main reported side effect and is described as harmless, though uncomfortable to some; divided or slow-release forms reduce it. Beta-alanine is legal and not banned in sport. Long-term data in healthy adults show no clear toxicity at studied intakes. Studies have found little effect on single-effort maximal strength, with benefits reported mainly for high-rep and endurance-type work.

lead: Beta-alanine is a naturally occurring non-proteinogenic amino acid in which the amino group sits on the beta carbon (IUPAC name 3-aminopropanoic acid) [1]. It is the rate-limiting precursor of carnosine, a dipeptide stored at high concentration in skeletal muscle, where it acts as an intramuscular buffer [1]. As a supplement it is sold as a powder or capsule and is a staple ingredient of pre-workout formulas.

It is used mainly in efforts lasting roughly 0.5 to 10 minutes and in high-repetition training, on the reasoning that more carnosine buffers hydrogen ions and delays neuromuscular fatigue [1]. Its best-known acute effect is paraesthesia, a dose-dependent tingling sensation of the skin [1].

Meta-analyses of placebo-controlled trials report small average benefits for exercise capacity, concentrated in efforts of about one to four minutes, with less consistent results for maximal-intensity and very short efforts [2][3]. It is not an agent that directly builds muscle tissue, and it is discussed in muscle-building communities chiefly as a performance and training-volume aid.
infobox: Glycine receptor agonist; GABA-A and GABA-C sites reported [1]

paras: Beta-alanine is taken by lifters, CrossFit-style athletes, rowers, runners and combat-sport athletes to support high-repetition sets and high-intensity intervals. Trials have tested it in high-intensity functional training, sport climbing, 10-km running time trials and multi-ingredient pre-workout products [4][5][6][7].
Because it does not directly add muscle, its place in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding forums is as an adjunct to training volume rather than an anabolic compound.

A 2023 narrative review assessed carnosine and beta-alanine supplementation in human medicine more broadly [8]. Registered trials have examined beta-alanine in adults with overweight or obesity and prediabetes (NCT05329610) and in cognition during a simulated military operation (NCT04250480) [9][10].

A 2017 systematic review and meta-analysis of 40 double-blind placebo-controlled studies (1,461 participants) concluded that beta-alanine supplementation has a small overall benefit for exercise measures [2]. A 2024 meta-analysis restricted to trained young men performing maximal or supramaximal efforts of 0.5 to 10 minutes (18 studies, 331 participants) found an overall effect size of 0.39 in favour of beta-alanine, with larger effects in efforts of 4 to 10 minutes [3].

A 2024 overview of sport supplements lists beta-alanine among a small set of supplements it covers [11]. Reviews of nutrition for female athletes have also considered it [12]. The International Society of Sports Nutrition has published a position stand on the supplement [13].

Individual studies report varied results. A multi-ingredient pre-workout study found that a blend containing beta-alanine and caffeine was compared with caffeine alone on bench press performance [4], and a study of acute pre-workout ingestion in basketball players tested a similar combination [14]. Because such products contain several active ingredients, the effect of beta-alanine alone cannot be isolated from them.

The only consistently reported adverse effect is paraesthesia, a tingling sensation that depends on dose [1]. Forum participants describe disliking this effect; one T Nation poster said they would prefer a beta-alanine-free version of a drink because of 'the tingles' [15]. Grokipedia states that splitting doses or using sustained-release forms reduces it, a claim attributed there to supplement research [16].

Wikipedia notes that no important adverse effects have been reported but that information on long-term use and on safety in combination with other supplements is lacking, and that many studies did not test supplement purity or for banned substances [1]. One forum user asked whether chronic supplementation could oversaturate carnosine and slow metabolism, citing a study on glucose uptake; the question was posed on T Nation without a published human study cited in support [17]. A registered trial examined 24 weeks of beta-alanine on muscle taurine and clinical blood parameters in healthy men (NCT03655041) [18].

Carnosine (beta-alanyl-L-histidine) occurs at about 17 to 25 mmol/kg dry muscle and contributes roughly 10 to 20 percent of buffering capacity in type I and II fibres; its imidazole group has a pKa near 6.8, suited to buffering [1]. Supplementing carnosine itself is less efficient because it is broken down into histidine and beta-alanine on digestion, so only about 40 percent of its weight is available as beta-alanine [1]. Human studies reported that oral beta-alanine raises muscle carnosine in the vastus lateralis and relates to high-intensity cycling capacity [19][20].

Beta-alanine is also a weak agonist at glycine receptors and has been reported to act at GABA-A, GABA-C and NMDA co-agonist sites, leading some authors to call it a putative small-molecule neurotransmitter [1].

It is formed endogenously from the breakdown of dihydrouracil and carnosine, can be transaminated with pyruvate, and is a component of pantothenic acid (vitamin B5) and so of coenzyme A [1]. A review of histidine metabolism describes the carnosine pathway [21].

Industrially it is produced from ammonia and beta-propiolactone according to Wikipedia [1]; Grokipedia describes ammoniation of acrylic acid [16]. Its formula is C3H7NO2 and it lacks a stereocentre [1][16].

Beta-alanine appears in many commercial pre-workouts. On T Nation, the site's own products include formulas with 2 g and 3.5 g of beta-alanine per serving, and its marketing describes carnosine increases of up to 58 percent in four weeks and 80 percent in ten weeks [22][23][24]. A product developer on the forum said the company discussed dosing with a beta-alanine researcher and described a cumulative loading approach [25]. Customers discuss out-of-stock products and tingling in the same threads [26][15].

Human trials are numerous and mostly small. Meta-analyses: 40 studies in 2017 [2] and 18 studies in trained men in 2024 [3]. Randomised trials include a 4-week study in high-intensity functional training participants measuring neuromuscular fatigue [5], a study in sport climbers [6], an acute pre-workout study in well-trained basketball players [14], a pre-workout blend versus caffeine bench-press crossover [4], and a trial of a 10-km running time trial in active adults [7]. Another trial combined nutritional supplementation with aerobic exercise to look at brain systems [27].

Registered trials cover muscle carnosine (NCT00813553), aerobic-anaerobic transition performance in endurance athletes (NCT05096793), CrossFit performance (NCT05772988), high-intensity interval training (NCT03708185), heart rate response (NCT01745016), tennis players (NCT05427409) and simulated wrestling matches (NCT07641907) [28][29][30][31][32][33][34].

lore.intro: Beta-alanine is discussed on T Nation mostly as one ingredient in pre-workouts, and 'the tingles' are a recurring topic of both fondness and complaint [15][17].

claims.claim: Beta-alanine raises muscle carnosine and so lets you do more work at high intensity
The tingling is a sign it is working
Chronic use could oversaturate carnosine and slow metabolism or cause fatigue
